props.title: The Amityville Horror

sections.content: The Amityville Horror (1979) revolutionized the haunted house genre by grounding supernatural terror in "based on true events" marketing. The film follows the Lutz family who move into 112 Ocean Avenue - a Dutch Colonial house where Ronald DeFeo Jr. murdered his family a year prior. Director Stuart Rosenberg crafts a slow-burning nightmare that plays on 1970s anxieties about home ownership and family stability. While The Exorcist (1973) had already proven supernatural horror could be prestigious, Amityville's "true story" approach sparked a wave of similarly marketed films like The Entity (1982) and A Haunting in Connecticut (2009).

sections.content: The film's lasting influence can be seen in countless haunted house movies that followed. The Conjuring (2013) directly references the Amityville case through its protagonists Ed and Lorraine Warren, who investigated the real Lutz house. The "flies scene" became iconic horror imagery, replicated in films like Candyman (1992) and Sinister (2012). James Brolin's descent into axe-wielding madness clearly influenced Jack Nicholson's performance in The Shining (1980), though Kubrick's masterpiece took the "haunted dad" trope to new psychological depths.

Beyond spawning numerous direct sequels and remakes, The Amityville Horror established key haunted house tropes: the too-good-to-be-true real estate deal, the skeptical family gradually accepting supernatural reality, and the house's dark history coming back to haunt new residents. These elements appear in everything from Burnt Offerings (1976) to The Others (2001) and Insidious (2010). The film's success also helped legitimize the paranormal investigation genre, paving the way for films like Grave Encounters (2011) and The Haunting in Connecticut (2009). sections.content: The genius of The Amityville Horror lies in its fusion of true crime and supernatural horror. The real DeFeo murders gave the supernatural elements a disturbing authenticity that pure fiction couldn't match. This approach influenced films like In the Dead of Winter (2014) and The Haunting of Sharon Tate (2019), which similarly blend historical tragedies with supernatural elements. Even found footage pioneers like Paranormal Activity (2007) owe a debt to Amityville's "this really happened" marketing strategy.
